parts.title: Your Crisper Drawer Has Two Jobs—and One Tiny Switch Decides Which
parts.part1:
A small slider inside your refrigerator may look unimportant.

“Low” on one side. “High” on the other.

But this simple control can help fresh food last longer.

Many crisper drawers offer low-humidity and high-humidity settings. Some refrigerators have two separate drawers. Others let users change the setting with a slider.

The key is not simply, “Fruit goes here, and vegetables go there.”

The real question is:

“Does this food release a lot of ethylene gas, or does it quickly lose water and wilt?”

Low-humidity drawers allow more air to move through. This matters because fruits release ethylene as they ripen. If nearby produce stays exposed to the gas, it may ripen too quickly and spoil.
parts.part2:
Foods that release a lot of ethylene, such as apples and pears, are better suited to the low-humidity drawer. The open vent helps the gas escape.

High-humidity drawers do the opposite. They stay more closed, so moisture remains inside.

That helps foods that lose water easily. Leafy greens such as kale can become soft and wilted when they dry out. Broccoli also benefits from high humidity for the same reason.

In other words, the two drawers manage two different kinds of escape.

In one drawer, gas needs a way out.

In the other, moisture needs to stay in.
parts.point_one_body: The common shortcut—fruit in low humidity and vegetables in high humidity—has important exceptions. Strawberries and citrus fruits, including oranges, prefer high humidity. UC Davis lists an ideal humidity of 90 to 95 percent for both. The food’s behavior matters more than its category.
parts.point_two_heading: Not every fresh food belongs in the drawer
parts.point_two_body: A humidity setting cannot fix the wrong storage location. Iowa State says tomatoes and bananas are better kept at room temperature, such as on a counter. Potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic do not need refrigeration. They prefer a cool, dry place instead.
parts.in_one_line: Let ethylene escape from one drawer and keep moisture inside the other—the food, not its label as a fruit or vegetable, should decide the setting.

parts.title: Two Drawers, Two Jobs: The Small Fridge Choice That Helps Produce Last
parts.part1:
The quiet problem starts after the shopping is done.

Fruit and vegetables go into the refrigerator. They may look safe inside the crisper drawer. But that drawer may have a small slider or dial. It is not just decoration.

Many refrigerators offer two settings: **high humidity** and **low humidity**. Each setting has a different job.

High humidity keeps the drawer more closed. This helps hold water around the food. It is useful for vegetables, especially leafy greens. These vegetables lose water quickly. When that happens, they become dry and wilt.
parts.part2:
Low humidity allows more air to move through the drawer. This is important for fruit.

As fruit becomes ripe, it gives off a natural gas called **ethylene**. If this gas stays around other fruit and vegetables, they may become ripe too quickly. Then they can go bad sooner.

A low-humidity drawer lets the gas escape more easily. This can help the food around the fruit last longer.

So the basic rule is simple:

**Fruit usually goes in low humidity. Vegetables, especially leafy greens, usually go in high humidity.**

It is a small change. But it gives each type of food the environment it needs.
parts.point_one_heading: The slider is really a small air door
parts.point_one_body: Think of the humidity control as a door for air. Low humidity opens the way for more airflow. High humidity keeps the drawer closer to sealed. KitchenAid and Whirlpool also recommend high humidity for leafy greens and low humidity for fruits such as apples and pears.
parts.point_two_heading: Some produce should skip the refrigerator
parts.point_two_body: Not every fruit or vegetable belongs in a crisper drawer. Iowa State University Extension says tomatoes, bananas, potatoes, sweet potatoes, onions, and garlic are not well suited to refrigerator storage. These foods are recommended for storage at room temperature instead.
parts.in_one_line: **Give leafy greens a closed, humid space, and give fruit an open path for its gas.** The right drawer can mean less wilting, slower spoilage, and produce that stays useful for longer.
